name: Worcester
headline: Getting to know Worcester,
street by street and hill by hill.
answer: Worcester is a city of 206,518 people (2020 Census) in Central Massachusetts and the historic seat of Worcester County. Its housing ranges from 19th-century triple-deckers to single-family homes, with 884 single-family sales in 2025. Worcester station at Union Station is the western end of the MBTA Framingham/Worcester Line to Boston, and I-290 runs through the city.
overview: Worcester was incorporated as a town in 1722 and became a city in 1848, and it has served as the seat of Worcester County since 1731. That long run shows in the streets: Victorian-era mill buildings, lunch-car diners and a large stock of triple-decker houses, a building type the city is often credited with originating. Downtown gathers around Worcester Common and Union Station in Washington Square, where the Framingham/Worcester Line begins its run east to Boston's South Station.

Open space threads through the city. Elm Park, whose first 27 acres were bought in 1854, carries a plaque calling it the first purchase of land for a public park in the United States. Mass Audubon's Broad Meadow Brook covers more than 400 acres of woods, fields and marsh, and Quinsigamond State Park offers swimming beaches and a 2,000-meter rowing course on Lake Quinsigamond. The Worcester Art Museum, open since 1898, holds nearly 40,000 objects, and colleges including Clark, Holy Cross and WPI sit across the city's hills.

housing.text: Worcester has many 19th-century triple-decker houses, a building type that likely originated in the city, along with Victorian-era mill buildings. Single-family homes are also traded in volume: The Warren Group counted 884 single-family sales in 2025.

name: Shrewsbury
headline: A closer look at Shrewsbury,
from the lakeshore to Main Street.
answer: Shrewsbury is a Worcester County town of 38,325 people (2020 Census), across Lake Quinsigamond from Worcester. Single-family homes grew along its 19th-century streetcar routes, and The Warren Group counted 234 single-family sales in 2025. I-290, Route 9, Route 20 and Route 140 cross the town; the nearest commuter rail stops are in neighboring Worcester, Grafton and Westborough.
overview: Shrewsbury sits just east of Worcester, with Lake Quinsigamond between them; I-290 crosses the water into town. Shrewsbury was incorporated in 1727 and grew along the old Boston Post Road, where two milestones from 1767 still stand. In the 19th century, streetcar lines helped single-family housing spread outward from the center, while the lakeshore filled with cottages and a summer resort season. The White City amusement park once stood by the lake; a shopping plaza holds the site today.

Main Street is the town's historic spine. The General Artemas Ward House Museum, a Harvard-affiliated house museum at 786 Main Street, opens for free guided tours from mid-April through November, across the road from Dean Park and its trails. Prospect Park adds 71 acres of forest paths, Jordan Pond has about 0.8 miles of trails, and Ski Ward at 1000 Main Street runs skiing, snowboarding and tubing through the year. The public library moved into a new 42,000-square-foot building in 2016.

name: Grafton
headline: Grafton, village by village,
from the common to the river.
answer: Grafton is a Worcester County town of 19,664 people (2020 Census) bordering Worcester, established in 1735. Its housing runs from the 19th-century homes around Grafton Common to worker housing in its Blackstone River mill villages. Grafton station in North Grafton is on the MBTA Framingham/Worcester Line, and Routes 122, 140 and 30 cross the town.
overview: Grafton's story begins with Hassanamisco, a Christian Indian plantation established in 1654; the town itself was established in 1735. Hassanamesitt Woods, about 200 acres on Keith Hill, is believed to hold the core of that Nipmuc village, and the Trust for Public Land bought it in 2004 for transfer to the town. Grafton Common, landscaped into an elliptical park in 1843 and 1844, is still ringed by a temple-front store, a mansard-roofed store and a Second Empire commercial block.

Away from the common, Grafton spreads into villages built on water power. North Grafton, once New England Village, sits where the Quinsigamond River falls more than 50 feet in a short distance, and Saundersville, Fisherville and Farnumsville line the Blackstone River in the southwest. Benjamin Willard began making clocks in a North Grafton workshop in 1766, a legacy now kept at the Willard House and Clock Museum. Grafton station on Pine Street puts the town on the Framingham/Worcester Line, and Tufts University's Cummings School of Veterinary Medicine has its campus here.

housing.text: The Massachusetts Historical Commission describes Grafton Center as possibly the best-preserved 19th-century residential and institutional village in its study area, while the Blackstone River villages retain much of their 19th-century worker housing, including duplexes, boardinghouses and double-deckers. Craftsman bungalows and Colonial Revival homes followed in the early 20th century.

name: Westborough
headline: Westborough, mapped out:
the center, the lake and the trails.
answer: Westborough is a Worcester County town of 21,567 people (2020 Census), incorporated in 1717. Its center keeps colonial and 19th-century homes, and The Warren Group counted 134 single-family sales in 2025. Westborough station is on the MBTA Framingham/Worcester Line, and the Massachusetts Turnpike, I-495 and Route 9 cross the town, linking it east to Boston and west to Worcester.
overview: Westborough was incorporated in 1717 as the hundredth town in Massachusetts, set off from Marlborough with twenty-seven families. Eli Whitney, later the inventor of the cotton gin, was born here in 1765, and a stone on Eli Whitney Street marks the spot. In 1810 the road between Boston and Worcester became an official turnpike through town, today's Route 9. Once the railroad came through the center, the commercial life of the town followed it, leaving brick blocks downtown and smaller turnpike villages like Wessonville.

The land is a broad central plain ringed by rounded hills, with a large cedar swamp at its eastern end and the Assabet River along part of the northern edge. Lake Chauncy, in the north, has a summer beach open to Westborough and Northborough residents and is used for swimming, boating and fishing. The Westborough Charm Bracelet, a roughly 28-mile loop trail developed since 2000 by the Westborough Community Land Trust and the town's Open Space Preservation Committee, links most of the major open spaces, with side trails planned to reach schools and neighborhoods.

housing.text: The Massachusetts Historical Commission notes two-story, center-chimney colonial houses, worker cottages grouped in the center and Italianate, Second Empire and Queen Anne houses on High Street. The Vintonville Historic District, just east of the center, is made up of modest houses on smaller lots, largely built between 1860 and 1890.

name: Holden
headline: Old mill villages and open hills,
just over the line from Worcester.
answer: Holden is a town of 19,905 people (2020 Census) in Worcester County, set in rolling hills just north of Worcester. Its houses range from 1800s mill-village homes to suburban streets that grew after World War II. Routes 122A, 31 and 68 cross the town, and the commuter rail stops at Worcester station next door.
overview: Holden covers about thirty-six square miles of rolling upland just north of Worcester, and the town notes that a good portion of that land is protected open space, watershed and recreation area. Settlement began around 1723, and Holden was incorporated on January 9, 1741, from what had been the north half of Worcester. Through the 1800s, mills grew up along the Quinapoxet River in villages such as Chaffin, Springdale and Dawsonville, while Jefferson became the industrial village in the south of town.

The landscape shifted again around 1900, when reservoirs built for Worcester and the Wachusett Reservoir project cleared most of the river mills. After World War II, Holden became largely residential. Holden Center is still the civic heart along Main Street, where the Gale Free Library has used the Damon Memorial building since 1888. For time outside, the 660-acre Trout Brook Recreation Area and the town beach at Eagle Lake are within town lines, and the Mass Central Rail Trail follows the Quinapoxet River into Holden from Oakdale in West Boylston.

housing.text: The Massachusetts Historical Commission's survey of Holden records one-story center-chimney Federal houses, mid-1800s side-passage houses with Greek Revival or Italianate trim, company tenements in Jefferson, and Bungalow and Four Square houses from 1915 to 1940, with suburban growth tied to Worcester after the 1920s. The town notes further residential growth after World War II.

name: Leominster
headline: A city that once made combs,
with a state forest at its back door.
answer: Leominster is a city of 43,782 people (2020 Census) in northern Worcester County, just south of Fitchburg. Its housing includes worker cottages, three-deckers and duplexes from its comb and plastics years. Route 2 and I-190 pass through, and North Leominster station is on the MBTA Fitchburg Line to Boston's North Station.
overview: Leominster grew out of Lancaster. Permanent settlement began around 1725, the town was established in 1740, and it became a city in 1915. Its factories gave it a distinct story: comb shops lined Exchange Street in Morse Hollow, and after celluloid was invented in 1868 Leominster became known as the Comb City. Plastics followed, and the plastic pink flamingo lawn ornament was invented here in 1956. John Chapman, the orchard planter known as Johnny Appleseed, was born here in 1774; a granite marker stands on Johnny Appleseed Lane.

Monument Square has been the civic and commercial center since the 1800s, and the railroad has run through North Leominster since 1841, where the commuter rail station now sits on Nashua Street. Open land is close. Leominster State Forest offers swimming at Crow Hill Pond, the Crow Hill Ledges and a stretch of the Midstate Trail. Sholan Farms, bought with the city's help, grows apples, berries and pumpkins on Pleasant Street. Phase One of the Twin Cities Rail Trail now links the business districts of Leominster and Fitchburg.

housing.text: The Massachusetts Historical Commission's survey of Leominster records worker cottages east of the center along Water, Spruce and Mechanic Streets and in Lincoln Terrace, along with double houses, gable-end duplexes and three-deckers, which it notes were especially common in the early 1900s. Larger Queen Anne and Colonial Revival houses line the West Side and the hillside streets northwest of Main Street.

name: Framingham
headline: Several old centers, one city,
on the road and rail line west of Boston.
answer: Framingham is a city of 72,362 people (2020 Census) in Middlesex County, on the main western corridor out of Boston. It grew from separate centers, including Saxonville, Framingham Centre and South Framingham, and its housing runs from mill-era double houses to two-families and suburban homes. Framingham station serves the Framingham/Worcester Line, and the Massachusetts Turnpike crosses the city.
overview: Framingham never had a single village at its heart. John Stone settled near the Sudbury River falls in 1647 and built a gristmill there, the start of what became the mill village of Saxonville. The town was incorporated in 1700, and Framingham Centre grew up as the civic focus on the old Boston turnpike. When the Boston and Worcester railroad reached South Framingham in 1834, that area became the industrial center. Voters approved a city charter in 2017, and Framingham became a city on January 1, 2018.

Those separate centers still shape the map. Saxonville keeps mid-1800s mill housing near the falls, and the Framingham Centre Common Historic District holds 28 buildings around the old common, including the Village Hall and First Parish Church. The Danforth Art Museum and School is now part of Framingham State University. Green space comes in several forms: Callahan State Park has more than 800 acres and seven miles of marked trails, Garden in the Woods shows New England native plants on 45 acres, and the Cochituate Rail Trail runs from Concord Street toward Natick.

housing.text: The Massachusetts Historical Commission's survey of Framingham records central-chimney double houses built for mill workers at Saxonville around 1825 to 1835, wood-frame tenements and row houses in South Framingham and Coburnville, and two-family houses that became common there in the early 1900s, with relatively few three-deckers. Larger suburban houses were built around Framingham Centre on Park Street, Prospect Street and Salem Road.

name: Marlborough
headline: A shoe-making city at the crossroads
of I-495 and I-290.
answer: Marlborough is a city of 41,793 people (2020 Census) in Middlesex County, where I-495 meets the eastern end of I-290. Its downtown grew from two 1800s shoe-making villages, and its housing includes three-deckers, double houses and converted factory condominiums. The city has no rail station; buses connect to Southborough and Framingham on the Framingham/Worcester Line.
overview: Families from Sudbury petitioned for a new town in 1656, and Marlborough was incorporated in 1660. The early settlement was largely destroyed during King Philip's War, then rebuilt along the Post Road, where George Washington stopped at Williams Tavern in 1789. Shoemaking defined the 1800s. Samuel and Joseph Boyd opened the first shoe business in 1836, factory output rose into the millions of dollars by 1865, and Marlborough incorporated as a city in 1890. Its land once also included today's Northborough, Southborough, Westborough, Berlin and Hudson.

Downtown took shape from two villages, an East Village along Main and Maple Streets and a West Village along Pleasant and Main, which grew together once the railroad ran between them. In 2014 the city created a 50-acre Downtown Village district to encourage mixed-use building, and some old shoe factories and churches nearby are now condominiums. The Assabet River Rail Trail heads north toward Hudson past an overlook above Fort Meadow Reservoir, and the 615-acre Desert Natural Area protects pitch pine and scrub forest on the Sudbury line.

housing.text: The Massachusetts Historical Commission's survey of Marlborough records central-chimney Colonial houses, Greek Revival and Italianate side-hall houses and cottages, wood-frame row and double houses, and three-deckers and apartment houses in the West Village and along Mechanic Street, with Dutch Colonial and bungalow houses from the early 1900s. The city's economic development office lists former factories and churches converted to condominiums.

name: Wakefield
headline: A lake to walk around,
a town to come home to.
answer: Wakefield is a Middlesex County town about 10 miles north of Boston, centered on Lake Quannapowitt and a downtown along Main Street. Single-family detached homes make up 55 percent of its housing, and about a third of its structures predate World War II. The Haverhill Line stops at Wakefield and Greenwood stations.
overview: Wakefield is a town of about 27,000 people, 10 miles north of Boston, and it is laid out around Lake Quannapowitt. A paved loop of about 3.6 miles circles the lake, and Wakefield Common sits at its southern end. From there, downtown runs south along Main Street toward Crystal Lake, the town's drinking-water reservoir. The town began as part of Reading. Its South Parish broke off as South Reading in 1812, and in 1868 the town took the name of Cyrus Wakefield, who gave land and money for a new town hall.

Two Haverhill Line stations, Wakefield and Greenwood, serve the town, and I-95/Route 128 runs along its northwest edge. Greenwood covers nearly all of southern Wakefield, while Montrose, Woodville and Lakeside fill in the east and north. On Saturdays from June through October, the farmers market sets up on North Avenue by Hall Park, on the lake's shore. Breakheart Reservation, a state park with two lakes and a swimming beach at Pearce Lake, has an entrance on Hemlock Road, the one closer to the beach.

housing.text: The town's Housing Production Plan for FY2026-2030 reports that single-family detached homes are 55 percent of all housing units, down from 62 percent in 2011, and that about a third of structures were built before World War II. Two-family homes, buildings of 20 to 49 units, and three- and four-unit buildings are the next most common types.

name: Reading
headline: A town common, a commuter line,
and woods a short walk from the front door.
answer: Reading is a Middlesex County town of 25,518 people (2020 Census) whose housing is mostly single-family, with a large share built before 1960. It grew around a traditional New England common and keeps conservation land such as the Town Forest. Reading station on the MBTA Haverhill Line runs to Boston's North Station, and I-93 and I-95/Route 128 cross the town.
overview: Reading began as an inland plantation for settlers from Lynn and was incorporated in 1644. Over the next two centuries it gave up land to form its neighbors: the parish to the south became South Reading and was renamed Wakefield in 1868, and the land north of the Ipswich River became North Reading in 1853. What remains centers on the Common, where Main and Salem Streets meet, framed by the First Congregational Church, the public library and the town hall.

The railroad reached Reading in 1845, and Woburn Street shows what followed: Queen Anne and Colonial Revival houses on well-proportioned lots along a tree-lined stretch, now a historic district. Around the built-up streets, Reading keeps a web of conservation land, from the Town Forest, its largest, to Bare Meadow and the Aberjona River Headwaters Trail through the Maillet Conservation Area.

housing.text: Reading's 2023 Housing Production Plan describes the housing stock as primarily single-family, at 76.7% of units, with 84.6% owner occupied. Over half of the homes were built before 1960, and about a third before 1940. The downtown area holds a number of multi-family, affordable and public housing developments.

name: Melrose
headline: Three train stops, one pond in the middle,
and Victorian streets that lead to the Fells.
answer: Melrose is a Middlesex County city of 29,817 people (2020 Census), about seven miles north of Boston. More than half its homes predate World War II, many Victorian near downtown and the rail line. Three MBTA Haverhill Line stations serve the city, and Oak Grove on the Orange Line sits just over the Malden border.
overview: Melrose was part of Charlestown and then Malden before it was incorporated as a town in 1850. When the Boston and Maine Railroad built three stops through it in 1845, houses followed the tracks, and in 1853 the town annexed the highlands from Stoneham. Melrose became a city in 1900. Its downtown, listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1982, runs along Main Street, and Ell Pond, the city's largest body of water, sits near the center with a gazebo and a new fountain.

The housing tells the city's history in layers. A 2022 housing plan found that most homes built before World War II cluster near downtown and the rail corridor, often in Victorian styles, while the eastern side filled in after the war with ranches and Capes. Larger buildings are concentrated downtown and along Main Street. At the edges are big green spaces: the eastern reaches of the Middlesex Fells, the Olmsted-designed Pine Banks Park on the Malden line, and Mount Hood, a city park and golf course with views toward Boston.

housing.text: Melrose's 2022 Housing Production Plan reports that 55% of homes are detached single-family and 11% are two-family, with 16% in buildings of 20 or more units. Over half were built before World War II, often in Victorian styles near downtown and the rail corridor; the eastern parts of the city saw more mid-century ranch and Cape houses after the war.

name: Stoneham
headline: A shoe town's square, a zoo by the pond,
and a third of the map left to the Fells.
answer: Stoneham is a Middlesex County town of 23,244 people (2020 Census), less than 10 miles northwest of Boston. About a third of its land lies in the Middlesex Fells Reservation. Slightly more than half its homes are single-family. I-93 runs through town, and Boston-bound rail stations sit in Melrose, Winchester and Malden next door.
overview: Early explorers called this land Charlestown End, and Governor Winthrop's party is said to have lunched by Spot Pond in 1632. Farmers settled slowly, and the town broke from Charlestown on December 17, 1725. A stagecoach line on the Medford to Andover Turnpike in 1833 brought house lots, and shoemaking grew from home workshops into more than forty manufacturers. That era left Central Square, with its Second Empire commercial blocks, the 1904 library, and churches lining the north side at Common Street.

A few blocks west of the square, Nobility Hill keeps Italianate, Stick and Queen Anne houses from about 1860 to 1920. The Middlesex Fells covers roughly a third of the town, with Spot Pond, Bear Hill and the Stone Zoo, founded in 1905. Stoneham's housing plan counts slightly more than half its homes as single-family, with much of the rest in larger buildings. The Tri-Community Greenway runs from Gould Street toward Woburn and Winchester.

housing.text: Stoneham's Housing Production Plan reports that 57.1% of housing units are single-family homes, and nearly half of the remaining multifamily units are in buildings of 20 or more units. About 65% of homes are owner-occupied. The plan points to the town center around Main Street as the area best suited for new housing.

name: Lowell
headline: Brick mills, working canals,
and a city still built around its river.
answer: Lowell is a Middlesex County city of 115,554 people (2020 Census), founded as a textile mill town and incorporated in 1826. Most of its housing was built before 1960, with a mix of multi-family buildings, duplexes, single-family homes and converted mills. The MBTA Lowell Line runs from Lowell station to Boston's North Station, and I-495 and US-3 cross the city.
overview: The first large textile mill went up in 1822 on land that would become Lowell, and the town of Lowell was incorporated on March 1, 1826, then chartered as a city in 1836. By the 1850s it had the largest industrial complex in the United States. Much of that landscape survives: Lowell National Historical Park, created in 1978, runs boat tours through the canal system and recreates 19th-century textile work in the Boott Cotton Mills Museum. Along the river, the Vandenberg Esplanade is part of the state's Lowell Heritage State Park.

Lowell's neighborhoods differ widely. Downtown, the Acre and Back Central hold most of the city's rental housing, while parts of Belvidere, Pawtucketville and the Highlands are mostly single-family streets. Beyond the mill core, the Lowell-Dracut-Tyngsboro State Forest, shared with two neighboring towns, adds about six miles of trails.

housing.text: Lowell's Housing Production Plan for 2024 to 2028 reports that 77% of the city's housing was built before 1960, with nearly a third predating 1900, and that 45% of units are in buildings of three or more units. Conversions of downtown buildings and mills account for much of recent production, and parts of Belvidere, Pawtucketville and the Highlands are predominantly single-family.

name: Newton
headline: Learn the villages first,
then find the street that fits.
answer: Newton is a city of thirteen villages in Middlesex County, about eight miles west of downtown Boston. Much of its housing is older: as of the 2000 Census, only 19 percent of its homes had been built after 1960. The Green Line D branch and the Framingham/Worcester commuter rail line connect it to Boston.
overview: Newton sits about eight miles west of downtown Boston and has no single center. Instead it is a patchwork of thirteen villages, from Auburndale and Waban to Nonantum and Chestnut Hill, and many of them have a small downtown of their own. The villages have no legal boundaries, so addresses can puzzle first-time visitors. The city goes by The Garden City. It began as Cambridge Village in 1681, took the name Newton in 1766 and became a city in 1874.

Water and transit shape the map. The Charles River runs along the city's north and west sides, past Newton Lower Falls and Newton Upper Falls, both former small industrial sites, and under Echo Bridge at Hemlock Gorge. The Green Line D branch runs through the middle of the city, with stops including Newton Centre and Riverside, while the Framingham/Worcester Line stops at Newtonville, West Newton and Auburndale. Commonwealth Avenue carries the Boston Marathon over Heartbreak Hill, between Walnut Street and Boston College.

housing.text: A 2003 city survey of mid-20th-century housing reported that, as of the 1960 Census, 70.5 percent of Newton's housing units were single-family dwellings and 20.5 percent were two-family homes. It also noted that, as of the 2000 Census, only 19 percent of the city's dwellings had been built after 1960.

name: Quincy
headline: Between the harbor and the hills,
a city with deep roots.
answer: Quincy is a coastal city in Norfolk County, on Boston Harbor, and the birthplace of John Adams and John Quincy Adams. About a third of its homes are detached single-family houses, and most of the rest are in buildings with two or more units. Four Red Line stations and three commuter rail lines connect it to Boston.
overview: Quincy calls itself the City of Presidents, and the reason is on Franklin Street: the houses where John Adams was born in 1735 and John Quincy Adams in 1767 still stand side by side there. The family's later home, the Old House at Peacefield, and its Stone Library are part of Adams National Historical Park. Quincy split from Braintree as a town in 1792 and became a city in 1888. Granite quarrying was its major industry for more than a century, and in 1826 the Granite Railway carried stone for the Bunker Hill Monument.

The shoreline runs from Squantum and Marina Bay around to Houghs Neck, with Wollaston Beach stretching about 2.3 miles along Quincy Shore Drive. Inland, the Blue Hills Reservation covers roughly a quarter of the city's land, and the old quarries in West Quincy are now a state reservation that climbers use. Four Red Line stations, North Quincy, Wollaston, Quincy Center and Quincy Adams, connect the city to Boston, and the Kingston, Greenbush and Fall River/New Bedford commuter rail lines all stop at Quincy Center.

housing.text: Housing Quincy, a 2022 study by the Metropolitan Area Planning Council, found that about a third of the city's housing units are detached single-family homes, two-thirds are in buildings with two or more units, and 63 percent were built after 1940. It describes the oceanfront areas of Squantum, Merrymount, Adams Shore and Houghs Neck as having predominantly older single-family housing.

name: Springfield
headline: Porches, parks and river light,
in a city that knows its neighborhoods.
answer: Springfield is the seat of Hampden County, on the eastern bank of the Connecticut River about 24 miles north of Hartford. Sixty-eight percent of its housing is single-family homes and duplexes, and 41 percent was built before 1940. Union Station offers Amtrak and Hartford Line trains, and I-91 and I-291 run through the city.
overview: Springfield sits on the eastern bank of the Connecticut River, about 24 miles north of Hartford, and serves as the Hampden County seat. William Pynchon founded it in 1636 as Agawam Plantation, and it became a city in 1852. The federal armory here began making small arms in 1794 and closed in 1968; its Main Arsenal now holds the National Park Service's collection of historic military firearms. James Naismith invented basketball in Springfield in 1891, and the Hall of Fame stands on the riverfront.

The city calls itself the City of Homes, a name tied to its Victorian houses. The McKnight Historic District, planned in 1881, has more than 900 of them, and the neighborhood around Forest Park has more than 600. Sixteen Acres holds much of the city's post-World War II building, and Indian Orchard grew up as its own mill town on the Chicopee River. Forest Park covers about 735 acres, with a zoo, Porter Lake and the Bright Nights holiday display. Union Station handles Amtrak, Hartford Line trains and intercity buses.

housing.text: The city's 2018 Housing Study found that 68 percent of Springfield's housing stock is single-family homes and duplexes, and that only 10 percent of units are in buildings with 20 or more units. It also found that 41 percent of units were built before 1940 and only 14 percent since 1980.

name: Boston
headline: Brownstones on filled marsh, three-deckers on the hills,
and every commuter rail line running home to it.
answer: Boston is the capital of Massachusetts, a Suffolk County city of 675,647 people (2020 Census) made up of 23 neighborhoods. Its housing is mostly attached and multi-unit: brownstone and brick row houses near the center, and triple-deckers, mostly built between the 1880s and 1930s, farther out. Single-family sales are a small and unrepresentative slice of the market: The Warren Group's Boston row counted 50 in 2025 against 1,611 condo sales, and it reports neighborhoods such as Dorchester, Jamaica Plain and Charlestown on separate rows. Every MBTA commuter rail line ends at South Station or North Station, and I-93 and I-90 meet downtown.
overview: Puritan settlers founded Boston on the Shawmut Peninsula in 1630, set aside Boston Common in 1634 and opened Boston Latin School in 1635. Much of today's city is made land: the South End was built on tidal marsh beginning in 1849, and the Back Bay was filled between 1857 and about 1882, which is why their streets run in regular grids of Victorian row houses. Boston became a city in 1822 and grew by annexation, taking in Dorchester in 1870 and Charlestown and West Roxbury, which included Jamaica Plain, in 1874.

The city recognizes 23 neighborhoods, from Beacon Hill and the North End to Hyde Park and West Roxbury. Frederick Law Olmsted's Emerald Necklace links about 1,100 acres of parks over 7 miles, from the Back Bay Fens through Jamaica Pond and the Arnold Arboretum to Franklin Park. The 2.5-mile Freedom Trail runs from downtown to the Bunker Hill Monument in Charlestown, and public ferries reach several of the Boston Harbor Islands. This is one city guide for now; neighborhood guides are planned.

housing.text: Boston's triple-deckers were mostly built between the 1880s and 1930s, and the city has studied new versions of the type for neighborhoods including Roxbury, Mattapan, Dorchester and Hyde Park. Near the center, the Back Bay, South End and Charlestown are known for 19th-century brownstone and brick row houses. Condominiums dominate sales: The Warren Group counted 1,611 condo sales and 50 single-family sales on its 2025 Boston row, so the single-family median of about $3.1 million describes a very small set of homes and not the city as a whole.

name: Cambridge
headline: Newtowne of 1630 on the Charles,
five Red Line stops and a reservoir to the west.
answer: Cambridge is a Middlesex County city of 118,403 people (2020 Census) on the north bank of the Charles River, across from Boston. Single-family homes are a small share of its housing: 6.4% of units, against 34.1% in buildings of more than 100 units, by the city's own count. The Warren Group recorded 105 single-family sales in 2025, a small market for a city of this size. Five Red Line stations run through Cambridge, from Alewife to Kendall/MIT, and Porter also has commuter rail.
overview: Cambridge was founded in December 1630 as Newtowne and renamed in May 1638 after the English university town, two years after the college that became Harvard was founded. George Washington took command of the Continental Army on Cambridge Common in 1775 and used the house at 105 Brattle Street as his first long-term headquarters during the siege of Boston. The West Boston Bridge of 1792 tied the town directly to Boston, and Cambridge became a city in 1846. MIT moved here from Boston in 1916.

The city recognizes 13 neighborhoods on about 6.4 square miles of land. Squares strung along Massachusetts Avenue anchor them: Harvard Square beside Harvard Yard, Central Square with City Hall, and Porter Square farther north, while Kendall Square grew from salt marsh and 19th-century industry into an office and laboratory district beside MIT. Cambridgeport keeps streets of triple-deckers near the river. In the west, Fresh Pond Reservation surrounds the city's drinking-water reservoir, and Mount Auburn Cemetery, founded in 1831, straddles the line with Watertown.

housing.text: By the city's inventory as of June 30, 2025, 6.4% of Cambridge's housing units are single-family homes, 11.9% are in two-unit buildings and 10.5% in three-unit buildings, while 34.1% are in buildings of more than 100 units. About two-thirds of occupied units (66.5%) are renter-occupied and 33.5% owner-occupied (2020 to 2024 American Community Survey). With so few single-family homes, The Warren Group's 105 single-family sales in 2025 reflect only a narrow part of the market.

Porter is also a Fitchburg Line commuter rail stop, about 15 minutes from Boston's North Station, and Lechmere in East Cambridge is on the Green Line. Route 2 enters at Alewife and runs with US 3 and Route 16 along Alewife Brook and Fresh Pond Parkways, then with US 3 along Memorial Drive beside the Charles.

name: Somerville
headline: A powder house, a hilltop castle,
and five Green Line stops opened in 2022.
meta: Somerville is a Middlesex County city of 81,045 people (2020 Census) just north of Cambridge and Boston. Triple-deckers, transit and 2025 prices, sourced.
answer: Somerville is a Middlesex County city of 81,045 people (2020 Census) on about 4.1 square miles of land just north of Cambridge and Boston, often described as the most densely populated municipality in New England. It is known for its triple-deckers, and since November 2023 three-unit buildings have been allowed citywide by right. The Warren Group counted only 72 single-family sales in 2025. Davis Square is on the Red Line, Assembly on the Orange Line, and five Green Line stations opened in 2022.
overview: Somerville was settled in 1629 as part of Charlestown and became its own town in 1842 and a city in 1872. Its hills played a part in the Revolution: British troops emptied the Old Powder House of gunpowder on September 1, 1774, setting off the Powder Alarm, and Prospect Hill was a Continental Army position during the siege of Boston, where tradition says Washington raised a flag on January 1, 1776. Brickmaking, meatpacking and a Ford assembly plant, open from 1926 to 1958, followed.

The city is organized around its squares. Davis Square, a six-point intersection named for grain dealer Person Davis, gained a Red Line station in 1984, and the Somerville Community Path runs from there on an old railroad right-of-way. Union Square, named for its Civil War recruiting role, and Ball Square have Green Line stations that opened in 2022, and Assembly Square on the Mystic River grew from the old Ford plant site into the Assembly Row development. The 2020 Census counted 36,269 housing units in the city.

housing.text: Somerville is known for its triple-deckers. In November 2023 the City Council made any three-unit building legal citywide by right, without zoning board approval, replacing 2019 rules that required a new triple-decker to sit next to an existing one and include an income-restricted unit. Single-family homes are a small part of the market: The Warren Group counted 72 single-family sales in 2025.

Rapid transit has returned in stages: Davis on the Red Line in 1984, Assembly on the Orange Line, and the Green Line Extension in 2022, with Union Square on one branch and East Somerville, Gilman Square, Magoun Square and Ball Square on the branch to Medford/Tufts. I-93 crosses the city on an elevated highway, Route 28 runs as McGrath Highway and Route 38 as Mystic Avenue.

name: Plymouth
headline: A harbor town of 1620,
with pine forest and ponds filling its western miles.
meta: Plymouth is a Plymouth County town of 61,217 people (2020 Census) on Cape Cod Bay, about 40 miles south of Boston. Homes, transit and 2025 prices, sourced.
answer: Plymouth is a Plymouth County town of 61,217 people (2020 Census) on Cape Cod Bay, about 40 miles south of Boston, and the largest municipality in Massachusetts by area. Founded by the Mayflower Pilgrims in 1620, it is one of the county's two seats. About 71 percent of its homes are detached single-family houses. Route 3 serves the town with six exits, and Plymouth's own commuter rail station has been suspended since 2021, so the nearest active stop is Kingston.
overview: The Mayflower Pilgrims settled here in December 1620, and Plymouth served as the capital of Plymouth Colony until 1691. The old town center keeps that story close to the water: Plymouth Rock under its 1921 portico in Pilgrim Memorial State Park, the Mayflower II at the State Pier, Cole's Hill, and Burial Hill above Leyden Street, where the Pilgrims built a fort in 1621 and 1622. Pilgrim Hall, opened in 1824 on Court Street, is the oldest public museum in the United States in continuous operation.

Beyond downtown the town spreads across about 96 square miles of land. North Plymouth grew around the Plymouth Cordage Company, once the largest maker of rope and twine in the world, and much of its multifamily housing evolved from mill housing. West Plymouth filled with subdivisions in the 1970s, and South Plymouth drew new growth from the 1980s. Inland, Myles Standish State Forest has ponds and pine and oak woods, while Manomet and Ellisville Harbor sit along the Cape Cod Bay shore.

housing.text: Plymouth's 2024 Housing Production Plan reports that detached single-family homes make up 71.1 percent of housing units, with attached single-family homes another 7.4 percent. As of 2021, 80.9 percent of occupied homes were owner-occupied, and the town's housing units grew from 25,058 in 2010 to 28,353 in 2021. The plan expects most new residential development in the town's rural areas, with recent projects in the south and at Cordage Park in the north.

name: Braintree
headline: Saltbox houses on Washington Street,
and a station where three rail lines meet.
answer: Braintree is a Norfolk County community of 39,143 people (2020 Census), about ten miles south of Boston, where I-93 and Route 3 meet. Most of its housing, 64 percent, is single-family detached homes. Braintree station on Ivory Street is served by the Red Line and two commuter rail lines, and the Greenbush Line stops at Weymouth Landing/East Braintree on the town line. It is legally a city with a mayor and council, though it keeps the name Town of Braintree.
overview: Braintree was colonized in 1635 and incorporated in 1640, and the old town once took in what are now Quincy, Randolph and Holbrook. The town counts John Adams, John Quincy Adams, John Hancock and General Sylvanus Thayer among those born in Old Braintree. Water power on the Monatiquot River drew mills to South Braintree in the 1820s, and the Old Colony railroad arrived there in 1845, making South Braintree a rail junction. East Braintree grew at the head of navigation on the Fore River.

Washington Street carries much of the town's older fabric, including the Thayer Birthplace, built in 1720, and the Asa French House, built about 1699, both now in the town's historic district. Open space includes the Town Forest, Sunset Lake, Smith Beach, the Cranberry Pond Conservation District and Pond Meadow Park, shared with Weymouth, along with an 18-hole public golf course. The town site describes established neighborhoods, small clusters of new homes and several condominium complexes.

housing.text: A 2024 town feasibility study reports that 64 percent of Braintree's housing is single-family detached units and that about 74 percent of units are owner-occupied. Only 12 percent of units are studios or one-bedrooms. The study counts a 5.42 percent increase in housing units from 2010 to 2020. The town also lists several condominium complexes among its housing.

name: Barnstable
headline: Seven villages between two shores,
from the Great Marsh to the Hyannis ferries.
answer: Barnstable is the seat of Barnstable County, a town of 48,916 people (2020 Census) made up of seven villages that run from Cape Cod Bay to Nantucket Sound. Detached single-family homes make up 84.8 percent of its residential properties, and the town's housing plan counts at least 23 percent of its housing units as second homes. Hyannis holds the town's transit links: the seasonal CapeFLYER train from Boston ends at the Hyannis Transportation Center, and ferries leave Hyannis for Nantucket and Martha's Vineyard. U.S. Route 6 crosses the town as a four-lane freeway.
overview: Bartholomew Gosnold explored this shore in 1602, and English settlers arrived on June 4, 1638, making Barnstable one of the first towns of Plymouth Colony; it was incorporated in 1639. The north side still follows the Old King's Highway, Route 6A, through Barnstable village and West Barnstable, where the 1644 house that forms the original part of the Sturgis Library is the oldest building housing a public library in the United States, and the Olde Colonial Courthouse recalls a 1774 protest led by James Otis and Samuel Adams. Behind them, Sandy Neck runs about six and a half miles along Cape Cod Bay, backed by salt marsh, with Sandy Neck Light at its tip.

The south side faces Nantucket Sound. Hyannis holds the historic Main Street, a large natural harbor and the ferry docks, along with Barnstable Municipal Airport and the Hyannis Transportation Center. West along Route 28, Centerville reaches Craigville Beach, Osterville keeps the Crosby boatbuilding story in its historical museum, and Cotuit sits on Cotuit Bay, the home water of the Cotuit oyster. Inland, Marstons Mills takes its name from Benjamin Marston's fulling mill and keeps a herring run, kettle ponds and a grass airfield dating to 1929.

housing.text: Barnstable's 2025 Housing Production Plan executive summary counts detached single-family homes as 84.8 percent of residential properties, and reports that at least 23 percent of the town's housing units are second homes. Hyannis holds about one-fifth of all housing units; single-family homes are 59 percent of its units, and most of its units are rented. The plan names town-owned sites in Marstons Mills, among others, for new year-round housing.

commute.text: Barnstable has no year-round passenger rail; the nearest year-round MBTA Commuter Rail stations are Middleborough and Kingston. In summer, the CapeFLYER runs weekends only from Memorial Day weekend through Labor Day between Boston's South Station and the Hyannis Transportation Center, with stops including Braintree, Brockton, Wareham Village, Buzzards Bay and Bourne. The Hyannis Transportation Center is also the terminal for Cape Cod Regional Transit Authority buses, including the Sealine to Falmouth and Woods Hole, and for Plymouth & Brockton and Peter Pan intercity buses. From Hyannis, the Steamship Authority runs year-round ferries to Nantucket and a seasonal high-speed passenger ferry, and Hy-Line runs passenger ferries to Nantucket and a seasonal catamaran to Martha's Vineyard. Barnstable Municipal Airport in Hyannis has scheduled flights to the islands and Boston. U.S. Route 6 crosses the town as a four-lane freeway, and Routes 132 and 149 link Route 6A to Route 28.

places.name: Osterville Historical Museum
places.line: A museum at 155 West Bay Road, founded in 1931, with the Cammett, Parker and Jelly houses and more than a dozen full-sized Crosby wooden boats.

places.name: Hyannis Harbor and Main Street
places.line: A large natural harbor, the Cape's largest recreational boating port, beside the historic downtown Main Street shopping district.

name: Falmouth
headline: A village green, a seaside bikeway,
and the ferry to the Vineyard at Woods Hole.
answer: Falmouth is an Upper Cape town of 32,517 people (2020 Census) in Barnstable County, bordered by Buzzards Bay to the west and Vineyard Sound to the south. Its 2024 Housing Production Plan counts 22,817 housing units, about 86 percent of them detached single-family homes, with 30 percent counted as seasonal units. Falmouth has no rail station: Steamship Authority ferries leave Woods Hole for Martha's Vineyard, and buses link the town to Hyannis and to Boston and Logan Airport. The median single-family sale price was $804,000 in 2025, across 424 sales.
overview: English colonists settled Falmouth in 1660, and the town was incorporated in 1686. Its center has gathered around a triangular village green since 1756, when the meeting house moved there, and late Colonial and Federal houses still frame it with the 1796 First Congregational Church on its north side. Katharine Lee Bates, who wrote the words to "America the Beautiful", was born on Main Street in 1859. Woods Hole was raided by British forces in 1779, and the Falmouth Heights shore was bombarded by British frigates in the War of 1812. By 1872 the railroad had reached Falmouth and Woods Hole.

That rail line is now the Shining Sea Bikeway, 10.7 miles from Route 151 in North Falmouth to the Steamship Authority dock in Woods Hole, with a stretch along the water. Woods Hole is a working science village: the Marine Biological Laboratory dates to 1888 and the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution to 1930, around the drawbridge at Eel Pond, with Nobska Light on the point above Vineyard Sound. Along the south shore, a run of closely spaced coastal ponds and necks leads east to the Waquoit Bay reserve, while West and North Falmouth face Buzzards Bay with harbors and public beaches such as Old Silver Beach.

housing.text: Falmouth's March 2024 Housing Production Plan counts 22,817 housing units in 2020, up from 18,168 in 1990. An estimated 86 percent are detached single-family homes, and 70 percent are counted as year-round units, with 30 percent counted as seasonal. The plan aims to direct new housing to areas that are already developed and to maximize affordable units on town-owned land.

villages.name: Woods Hole

villages.name: North Falmouth

name: New Bedford
headline: Cobblestones above the working harbor,
and the train back on Acushnet Avenue.
answer: New Bedford is a Bristol County city of 101,079 people (2020 Census) on the Acushnet River where it meets Buzzards Bay. Its downtown waterfront is part of New Bedford Whaling National Historical Park, established in 1996. The Warren Group counted 401 single-family sales in 2025. Since March 24, 2025, the MBTA Fall River/New Bedford Line has run from New Bedford and Church Street stations to Boston's South Station, and I-195 crosses the city.
overview: New Bedford was incorporated as a town in 1787 and became a city in 1847. In the first half of the 1800s it was one of the world's most important whaling ports, and in 1857 its harbor counted 329 vessels. The downtown historic district, 11 city blocks and part of a twelfth west of the waterfront, keeps Federal and Greek Revival buildings put up mostly between 1790 and 1855, including Seamen's Bethel and the 1836 U.S. Customhouse. Frederick Douglass settled in the city in 1838 and lived there until 1841.

When whaling faded, cotton mills took over, and the Wamsutta Mills were for a time the world's largest weaving plant. The housing that followed spreads out from downtown: the County Street Historic District, laid out in the 18th century, holds City Hall, the library and large houses in Greek Revival and Gothic Revival styles, while Acushnet Heights keeps wood-frame houses built for factory workers from the 1860s on. Buttonwood Park and its zoo sit to the west, and Fort Taber Park occupies Clark's Point, the city's southern tip on Buzzards Bay.

housing.text: The 2020 Census counted 42,781 housing units in New Bedford, about 2,063 per square mile, and 39,208 households. Older neighborhoods mix 19th-century wood-frame houses with downtown commercial and mixed-use blocks, and The Warren Group recorded 401 single-family sales in 2025.

name: Fall River
headline: Granite mills on a falling river,
a battleship at the foot of the hill.
answer: Fall River is a Bristol County city of 94,000 people (2020 Census) on the Taunton River and Mount Hope Bay, at the Rhode Island line. It grew into a leading U.S. textile city in the 1800s, and its housing still includes many 19th-century triple-deckers. The Warren Group counted 300 single-family sales in 2025. Since March 24, 2025, Fall River Depot station has linked the city to Boston's South Station on the MBTA Fall River/New Bedford Line, and I-195 and Route 24 meet here.
overview: Fall River separated from Freetown as a town in 1803, spent about 30 years named Troy, and took back its name in 1834; it became a city in 1854. The name comes from the Quequechan River, believed to mean 'falling river' in Wampanoag. A fire in July 1843 destroyed much of the town center, and the city motto, 'We'll Try', dates from the rebuilding. Mills followed the river's drop to the bay, and by 1868 the city had passed Lowell as the leading U.S. textile city. The 1847 Metacomet Mill is its oldest surviving textile mill.

I-195 divides the city into the North End and the South End. North of the highway, the Highlands ridge keeps houses from about 1840 to 1925 in Greek Revival, Italianate, Second Empire and Queen Anne styles, along with North Park, designed by the Olmsted Brothers. Below it, the Lower Highlands mixes Federal and Greek Revival houses with late-19th-century multiunit worker housing. On the waterfront, Battleship Cove and Fall River Heritage State Park sit beside the Braga Bridge, and to the south Kennedy Park, designed by Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux, slopes down to Mount Hope Bay.

housing.text: Fall River's mill boom housed workers in thousands of wood-frame, multi-family tenements, usually three-floor triple-deckers with up to six apartments, and mill companies built more than 12,000 units. The Highlands and Lower Highlands keep older single-family and Victorian houses, and The Warren Group recorded 300 single-family sales in 2025.

name: Pittsfield
headline: A county seat around Park Square,
with two lakes and a state forest at its edges.
answer: Pittsfield is a city of 43,927 people (2020 Census) and the seat of Berkshire County. A city housing analysis describes its homes as mostly single-family houses and small two- and three-unit buildings, and The Warren Group counted 434 single-family sales in 2025. Amtrak's Lake Shore Limited stops at the Joseph Scelsi Intermodal Transportation Center, and the seasonal Berkshire Flyer runs from there to New York. US 7 and US 20 meet in the city, and the Massachusetts Turnpike is about 10 miles south in Lee.
overview: Settlement here dates to 1752, and the plantation of Pontoosuc was organized in 1753 before being incorporated as a town in 1761 and named for William Pitt. Park Square was laid out in 1790 on donated land, and the Old Town Hall, the county courthouse, the Berkshire Athenaeum and the First Church of Christ still face it. Late in the 19th century downtown pushed north along North Street, helped by an 1891 trolley line. In 1890 William Stanley Jr. founded the Stanley Electric Manufacturing Company here, and General Electric bought it in 1903. Pittsfield became a city in 1891.

Water and woods frame the city. Onota Lake, 617 acres and owned by the city, and Pontoosuc Lake are used for swimming, boating and fishing, and Pittsfield State Forest covers 11,000 acres with Berry Pond and 30 miles of trails. Herman Melville finished Moby-Dick at Arrowhead, his home on Holmes Road from 1850 to 1863. On West Housatonic Street, Hancock Shaker Village keeps 20 historic buildings, including a round stone barn from 1826. Downtown, the Colonial Theatre of 1903 reopened after restoration in 2006, and the Berkshire Museum, founded by Zenas Crane in 1903, holds more than 40,000 objects.

housing.text: A 2009 city housing analysis describes Pittsfield's housing stock as relatively old, made up mainly of single-family homes and small multifamily buildings of two or three units, and counted 21,633 units citywide in 2008. In the Westside and Morningside neighborhoods next to downtown, more than 80% of homes were built before 1969, and many larger houses from the 1890s to 1930s have been divided into apartments.

name: Great Barrington
headline: A Main Street on the Housatonic,
and Monument Mountain up Route 7.
answer: Great Barrington is a Berkshire County town of 7,172 people (2020 Census) in the Housatonic River valley. US 7 runs through its center as Main Street, and the town also takes in the villages of Housatonic and Van Deusenville. There is no passenger rail station in town; BRTA buses run to Lee and to Pittsfield, where Amtrak stops. The Warren Group counted 77 single-family sales in Great Barrington in 2025.
overview: The Mahican name for this stretch of the river was Mahaiwe, "the place downstream." Colonists settled here in 1726, the area served as the north parish of Sheffield from 1742, and it was incorporated as Great Barrington in 1761. In 1774 local colonists forced the Berkshire County court to close in protest of British policy, and in March 1886 William Stanley's alternating current system lit 23 businesses along Main Street. That Main Street still carries US 7 through the central village, where the Mahaiwe Theater opened in 1905 and reopened in 2005 as a performing arts center.

North of the center, the village of Housatonic grew in the early 1800s around textile and paper mills on the river; Monument Mills, which had 500 employees at its peak, closed in 1956, and the mill buildings are listed on the National Register. Monument Mountain rises along Route 7, with 503 acres and a 1,642-foot summit kept by The Trustees. To the east, East Mountain holds Ski Butternut and a state forest crossed by the Appalachian Trail. The Housatonic River Walk follows the river through downtown, and the W. E. B. Du Bois Boyhood Homesite, a National Historic Landmark, lies on the road to South Egremont.

housing.text: Seasonal use shapes Great Barrington's housing. In December 2025 the Commonwealth identified the town as eligible for its Seasonal Communities designation, whose criteria include the share of housing units used for seasonal, recreational or occasional use. Annual Town Meeting voters accepted the designation on May 2, 2026, and the Selectboard and Planning Board scheduled a joint meeting on related zoning changes for June 1, 2026.
